title: Phagocyte Defects: LAD Types 1 and 2, Chédiak-Higashi, and DHR versus NBT
summary: Learn how leukocyte adhesion deficiency types 1 and 2 and Chédiak-Higashi syndrome break neutrophil function, which lab test points to each, and why the flow-cytometric DHR assay has replaced the NBT slide for CGD.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 52 Hit 10 (LAD type 1 = CD18; LAD type 2 = sialyl Lewis X and Bombay), Hit 11 (Chédiak-Higashi) and Trap 3 (NBT versus DHR), checked against Das 2020 and Kambli 2020 (LAD), Lozano 2014 (Chédiak-Higashi) and Yu 2018 (CGD testing). Hit 10 links the Bombay phenotype to defective sialyl Lewis X; Das 2020 traces both to a GDP-fucose transporter defect (register flag rv-lad2-fucose-transporter). Hit 11 omits the HLH accelerated phase and the platelet bleeding tendency, and calls the neutropenia “mild” where Lozano 2014 says moderate or transient (register flag rv-chs-accelerated-phase). Not taught: the dichlorofluorescein diacetate alternative named in Hit 3 and Trap 3 (no source read), LAD type 4, therapy details.

objectives: Explain how loss of CD18 in LAD type 1 and loss of fucosylated selectin ligands in LAD type 2 block neutrophil exit from the blood.
Recognise Chédiak-Higashi syndrome from giant granules, partial albinism and its accelerated phase.
Explain why the flow-cytometric DHR assay has largely replaced the NBT slide test for CGD, and its myeloperoxidase-deficiency pitfall.

scenes.title: Three children, three phagocyte puzzles
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three children referred for recurrent bacterial infections — (1) a 4-week-old whose umbilical cord is still attached, with omphalitis but no pus and a white count of 40,000/µL, mostly neutrophils; (2) a 4-year-old with silvery hair, pale skin and repeated staphylococcal skin infections, whose blood smear shows giant granules in the neutrophils; (3) a 2-year-old with Aspergillus pneumonia, for whom the lab can offer an NBT slide test or a DHR flow assay. Question token: “Which defect, and which test?”

cues.text: Three children with recurrent bacterial infections. The first is four weeks old, the cord is still attached, the navel is infected but there is no pus, and the white count is forty thousand.
The second has silvery hair, pale skin and repeated staph skin infections, and the smear shows giant granules in the neutrophils. The third has Aspergillus pneumonia.
Which defect does each child have, and for the third, which test should the lab run?

scenes.title: How a neutrophil gets out and kills
scenes.altText: Schematic leukocyte adhesion cascade in a blood vessel. Step 1, rolling: selectins (P- and E-selectin) on activated endothelium bind fucosylated sialyl Lewis X (CD15s) on the leukocyte. Step 2, firm arrest: chemokines activate β2 integrins (a CD11 alpha chain paired with the common CD18 beta chain), which bind ICAMs on endothelium; kindlin-3 is needed for this activation. Step 3, transmigration into the tissue, where pus forms. Inside the tissue, the neutrophil engulfs microbes and kills them with granule contents and the NADPH oxidase respiratory burst.

cues.text: A neutrophil has to leave the blood before it can fight. First it rolls: selectins on inflamed endothelium catch a sugar on the neutrophil called sialyl Lewis X, CD15s, which needs fucose.
Next it stops. Chemokines switch on beta-2 integrins: a CD11 chain paired with a shared CD18 chain. These bind ICAMs on the vessel wall, and an adaptor called kindlin-3 is needed for the switch.
Then it squeezes between endothelial cells into the tissue, where neutrophils gather as pus.
Once there, it engulfs the microbe and kills it with its granule contents and the oxidative burst made by NADPH oxidase.

scenes.title: Three ways the neutrophil fails
scenes.altText: Three cards. LAD type 1: autosomal recessive ITGB2 mutation, loss of CD18, the shared beta chain of the β2 integrins; neutrophils cannot adhere and leave the blood, so there is persistent neutrophil leukocytosis (usually above 15,000/µL) even without infection, infections without pus, delayed separation of the umbilical cord with omphalitis, and poor wound healing; severity tracks CD18 expression (under 2% severe, 2–30% moderate, above 30% mild). LAD type 2: SLC35C1 mutation in the Golgi GDP-fucose transporter, so fucosylated sugars are missing — no sialyl Lewis X (rolling fails) and no H antigen on red cells (Bombay phenotype); milder infections, growth and intellectual disability, no delayed cord separation, wound healing not impaired. LAD type 3 (kindlin-3) has normal CD18 but bleeding like Glanzmann thrombasthenia. Chédiak-Higashi syndrome: autosomal recessive LYST (CHS1) mutation; giant granules in neutrophils, lymphocytes and NK cells; partial oculocutaneous albinism with silvery hair; pyogenic infections (Staphylococcus, Streptococcus); neutropenia; mild bleeding from platelets with reduced dense granules; peripheral neuropathy and later neurologic decline; an accelerated phase of hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) in 50–85% of patients.

cues.text: Lose CD18 and you have leukocyte adhesion deficiency type one, an autosomal recessive defect of the ITGB2 gene. Neutrophils cannot stick, so they stay in the blood: a high neutrophil count even without infection, infections without pus, delayed cord separation and poor wound healing.
The less CD18 on the cells, the more severe the disease. CD18 expression under two percent is classed as the severe form.

Type two is a fucose problem: a broken Golgi transporter for GDP-fucose. No sialyl Lewis X means no rolling, and no H antigen on red cells gives the Bombay phenotype. Infections are milder, and the cord falls off on time.

Chédiak-Higashi is a lysosome trafficking defect in the LYST gene. Giant granules fill neutrophils, lymphocytes and NK cells, with partial albinism, pyogenic infections, mild bleeding and nerve damage. Most patients reach an accelerated phase of hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis.

scenes.title: Matching each defect to its test
scenes.altText: Test cards. LAD type 1: flow cytometry for CD18 and CD11 on neutrophils; gene testing for ITGB2 confirms. LAD type 2: flow cytometry for sialyl Lewis X (CD15) on neutrophils; SLC35C1 testing confirms. Chédiak-Higashi: giant granules on a Wright-Giemsa smear (often found incidentally); hair shows clumped melanin; LYST gene testing gives the definite diagnosis. CGD comparison card: NBT slide test — PMA-stimulated neutrophils reduce yellow nitroblue tetrazolium to dark-blue formazan, read by microscope; semiquantitative, technician-dependent, needs fresh blood, often misses carriers. DHR assay — PMA-stimulated neutrophils oxidise dihydrorhodamine 123 to fluorescent rhodamine 123 using hydrogen peroxide from the NADPH oxidase–myeloperoxidase system, read by flow cytometry; quantitative, more sensitive, usually separates X-linked CGD, autosomal recessive CGD and X-linked carriers; since the late 1990s it has largely superseded NBT. Complete myeloperoxidase deficiency typically gives an abnormal DHR but a normal NBT. Hook answers: (1) LAD type 1, check CD18 by flow; (2) Chédiak-Higashi; (3) DHR flow assay.

cues.text: Each defect has its own lab clue. For type one, flow cytometry usually shows reduced or absent CD18 and CD11 on neutrophils. For type two, flow shows missing sialyl Lewis X, CD15. Gene testing confirms both.
Chédiak-Higashi is often spotted on the smear: giant granules in the neutrophils. Gene testing for LYST is the definite diagnosis.

For chronic granulomatous disease, the old NBT slide turns a yellow dye dark blue inside working neutrophils and is read by eye. The DHR assay makes working neutrophils fluoresce and is read by flow cytometry. It is quantitative, more sensitive, and can spot X-linked carriers, so it has largely replaced NBT.

One catch: myeloperoxidase deficiency can also give an abnormal DHR, but a normal NBT. Back to the hook: child one has LAD type one, child two has Chédiak-Higashi, and child three needs the DHR assay.

props.title: MPO deficiency: DHR abnormal, NBT normal

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “The NBT slide test is the modern screen for CGD” (✓ flow-cytometric DHR has largely superseded NBT since the late 1990s); “Every LAD type delays cord separation” (✓ LAD type 1 and type 3 do; LAD type 2 does not); “An abnormal DHR always means CGD” (✓ myeloperoxidase deficiency can also give an abnormal DHR, with a normal NBT).

cues.text: Trap one: the NBT slide is the modern screen for chronic granulomatous disease. No: the flow-cytometric DHR assay has largely replaced it.
Trap two: every leukocyte adhesion deficiency delays cord separation. No: types one and three do, but type two does not.
Trap three: an abnormal DHR always means chronic granulomatous disease. No: myeloperoxidase deficiency can also give an abnormal DHR, while its NBT is normal.

lines: ✓ DHR flow assay has largely replaced it

props.title: ✗ “Abnormal DHR = CGD, always.”

scenes.title: Velcro, sugar, balloons
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “LAD type 1 has lost its VELCRO (CD18), so neutrophils cannot grip the vessel wall and pile up in the blood; LAD type 2 has lost the fucose SUGAR coat, so it cannot roll and its red cells lose H antigen (Bombay); Chédiak-Higashi cells carry giant BALLOON granules.” Tokens: Velcro = CD18 · Sugar = fucose · Balloons = giant granules. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: velcro, sugar, balloons. Type one has lost its velcro, CD18, so neutrophils cannot grip the vessel wall. Type two has lost its fucose sugar coat, so it cannot roll, and red cells lose H antigen. Chédiak-Higashi cells carry giant balloon granules.

Where it breaks: the neutrophils are not glued in place, they circulate but cannot leave; LAD type three has normal CD18 yet still fails to grip; and in Chédiak-Higashi the giant granules are not the main danger, the accelerated phase is.

props.title: Where it breaks
lines: Cells circulate; they just cannot exit
LAD 3: normal CD18, still no grip
CHS: the HLH phase is the real threat

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “LAD 1 = no CD18, neutrophilia without pus · LAD 2 = no fucose, Bombay · CHS = giant granules, albinism”, “CGD screen: DHR by flow, not the NBT slide”.

cues.text: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1 lacks CD18 so neutrophils pile up in the blood without forming pus, type 2 lacks fucosylated sialyl Lewis X and H antigen, Chédiak-Higashi syndrome shows giant granules with partial albinism, and the flow-cytometric DHR assay has largely replaced the NBT slide for chronic granulomatous disease.

props.label: LAD 1 = no CD18 · LAD 2 = no fucose, Bombay · CHS = giant granules
CGD screen: DHR by flow cytometry, not the NBT slide

explanation.what: Plain language: neutrophils must roll along, stop on, and squeeze through the blood-vessel wall before they can fight infection, and then they must kill what they eat. In LAD type 1 the grip molecule is missing, in LAD type 2 the sugar used for rolling is missing, and in Chédiak-Higashi the granules are giant and do not work properly. Scientific terms: leukocyte adhesion cascade, selectins, sialyl Lewis X (CD15s), β2 integrin (CD11/CD18), ITGB2, SLC35C1 GDP-fucose transporter, kindlin-3 (FERMT3), H antigen and Bombay phenotype, LYST (CHS1), giant granules, partial oculocutaneous albinism, hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH), nitroblue tetrazolium (NBT), dihydrorhodamine 123 (DHR), myeloperoxidase (MPO).
explanation.why: Neutrophils that cannot adhere stay in the circulation, so the blood count rises while tissues go undefended and no pus forms. Fucose is needed both for selectin ligands and for H antigen, so one transporter defect produces both a rolling defect and a Bombay red-cell type. In Chédiak-Higashi, abnormal lysosome trafficking gives giant granules, defective killing and cytotoxicity, and a predisposition to HLH.
explanation.measure: LAD type 1: flow cytometry for CD18 (with CD11) on neutrophils; in one cohort classification CD18 expression under 2% is severe, 2–30% moderate and above 30% mild, though CD18 results do not always match the genotype; ITGB2 gene testing confirms. LAD type 2: flow cytometry for sialyl Lewis X (CD15); SLC35C1 testing confirms. Chédiak-Higashi: giant granules on the blood smear; LYST testing is definitive. CGD: DHR flow assay (PMA-stimulated; DHR 123 oxidised to fluorescent rhodamine 123) rather than the semiquantitative NBT slide.
explanation.differs: LAD type 1 (no CD18, delayed cord separation, poor wound healing) vs LAD type 2 (no fucosylated ligands, Bombay, cord on time, wound healing intact) vs LAD type 3 (normal CD18, bleeding); NBT (microscopic, semiquantitative, often misses carriers) vs DHR (flow, quantitative, usually separates X-linked, recessive and carrier patterns); CGD (abnormal DHR and NBT) vs MPO deficiency (abnormal DHR, normal NBT).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: an infant with delayed cord separation, marked neutrophilia and no pus (LAD type 1, CD18 flow); a child with silvery hair and giant granules (Chédiak-Higashi); LAD with Bombay phenotype (type 2); or which test is the modern CGD screen (DHR).

mnemonic.text: Velcro, sugar, balloons: LAD type 1 has lost its VELCRO (CD18), LAD type 2 has lost its fucose SUGAR coat (no rolling, no H antigen), and Chédiak-Higashi cells carry giant BALLOON granules.
mnemonic.explanation: Ties each disorder to the one structure that fails.
mnemonic.limitation: LAD neutrophils are not glued in place; they circulate but cannot leave the vessel. LAD type 3 has normal CD18 yet still cannot grip. In Chédiak-Higashi the giant granules are a marker; the life-threatening problem is the HLH accelerated phase.

takeaway: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1 lacks CD18 so neutrophils pile up in the blood without forming pus, type 2 lacks fucosylated sialyl Lewis X and H antigen, Chédiak-Higashi syndrome shows giant granules with partial albinism, and the flow-cytometric DHR assay has largely replaced the NBT slide for chronic granulomatous disease.

questions.stem: A 3-week-old has an infected umbilical stump with no pus, the cord has not yet separated, and the white count is markedly raised with mostly neutrophils, with no other source of infection found. Which test best supports the likely diagnosis?

options.text: Flow cytometry for CD18 expression on neutrophils
options.rationale: Correct. Delayed cord separation, infection without pus and persistent neutrophilia suggest LAD type 1; absent or reduced CD18 on flow cytometry supports it, and ITGB2 testing confirms.
Incorrect. DHR tests the oxidative burst for CGD; it does not detect the adhesion defect.
Incorrect. Giant granules point to Chédiak-Higashi syndrome; delayed cord separation, infection without pus and marked neutrophilia are the LAD pattern.

options.text: Red-cell typing for the Bombay phenotype
options.rationale: Incorrect. Bombay red cells point to LAD type 2, in which the umbilical cord separates on time.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old with silvery hair, light skin and recurrent staphylococcal skin infections has neutrophils packed with giant cytoplasmic granules on a Wright-Giemsa smear. Which statement about the likely disorder is correct?

options.text: Most patients develop an accelerated phase of hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis
options.rationale: Correct. This is Chédiak-Higashi syndrome; the HLH accelerated phase affects most patients and is fatal unless treated, which is why early transplantation is considered.

options.text: It is caused by loss of the CD18 integrin chain
options.rationale: Incorrect. That is LAD type 1. Chédiak-Higashi is caused by mutations in the lysosomal trafficking gene LYST.

options.text: The NBT test will show no dye reduction
options.rationale: Incorrect. Failure to reduce NBT is the classic finding in CGD, a defect of NADPH oxidase; Chédiak-Higashi is a lysosomal trafficking defect.

options.text: Giant granules are found only in neutrophils
options.rationale: Incorrect. Giant granules are seen in virtually all granulated cells, including lymphocytes and NK cells.

questions.stem: Why has the flow-cytometric dihydrorhodamine (DHR) assay largely replaced the nitroblue tetrazolium (NBT) slide test for diagnosing CGD?

options.text: It is quantitative and more sensitive, and usually separates X-linked CGD, recessive CGD and X-linked carriers
options.rationale: Correct. NBT is read by eye, is semiquantitative and technician-dependent, and often misses carriers; DHR gives a flow-cytometric fluorescence measurement.

options.text: It measures phagocytosis rather than the oxidative burst
options.rationale: Incorrect. Both tests measure oxidative burst (NADPH oxidase) activity in stimulated neutrophils; neither measures phagocytosis.

options.text: It does not need the neutrophils to be stimulated
options.rationale: Incorrect. Neutrophils are stimulated with PMA in both the DHR and NBT tests.

options.text: It cannot be affected by myeloperoxidase deficiency
options.rationale: Incorrect. Myeloperoxidase deficiency can give an abnormal DHR result, so an abnormal DHR is confirmed by gene testing; the NBT test is normal in that disorder.

claims.text: Leukocyte adhesion cascade: selectin–sialyl Lewis X rolling, integrin activation via kindlin-3, β2 integrin–ICAM arrest, transmigration.
LAD type 1: autosomal recessive ITGB2/CD18 defect; persistent neutrophilia, absent pus, delayed cord separation, poor wound healing; CD18 flow cytometry with severity bands; ITGB2 testing confirms.
LAD type 2: SLC35C1 GDP-fucose transporter defect; absent sialyl Lewis X and H antigen (Bombay); milder infections; no delayed cord separation; wound healing intact; CD15 flow cytometry.
LAD type 3: kindlin-3 defect, normal CD18, bleeding like Glanzmann thrombasthenia.

Chédiak-Higashi: autosomal recessive LYST defect; giant granules in neutrophils, lymphocytes and NK cells; partial albinism, silvery hair; pyogenic infections; neutropenia; mild bleeding from platelets with reduced dense granules; peripheral neuropathy; HLH accelerated phase in 50–85%; diagnosis by smear and LYST testing.
NBT and DHR principles; DHR largely superseded NBT; DHR separates X-linked, recessive and carrier patterns; MPO deficiency gives abnormal DHR with normal NBT.
Dichlorofluorescein diacetate as an alternative flow-cytometric burst probe (reviewer Hit 3 and Trap 3).

claims.text: Scenario invented; vessel, cells and granules schematic.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 52 Hit 10 writes “LAD type 2 = defective sialyl-Lewis X → Bombay blood group”, implying the missing selectin ligand causes the Bombay phenotype. Das 2020 traces both to one defect in fucose metabolism (the Golgi GDP-fucose transporter, SLC35C1): sialyl Lewis X and H antigen are separate fucosylated structures that are both lost (register flag rv-lad2-fucose-transporter).

Ch. 52 Hit 11 lists giant granules, partial albinism, peripheral neuropathy and “mild” neutropenia but omits the accelerated phase (HLH, in 50–85% of patients and fatal untreated) and the mild bleeding tendency from platelets with reduced dense granules; Lozano 2014 describes the neutropenia as moderate or transient (register flag rv-chs-accelerated-phase).

morphology.note: No micrographs; cells, granules and tests are shown as schematic cards.

verification.notes: Six factual claims checked against Das 2020, Kambli 2020, Lozano 2014 and Yu 2018 (all read as Europe PMC full text). One reviewer claim (dichlorofluorescein alternative) is pending and not taught. No human expert has reviewed this lesson.
